rv.q: Caryl Churchill's latest play is a masterpiece of economy and precision, building to a devastating climax that feels both inevitable and shocking.

The Children — which premiered at the Royal Court in London last year and has now transferred to Broadway’s Samuel J. Friedman Theatre with its original cast and deft, deceptively unostentatious director, James Macdonald — is a play about responsibility and guilt, reparation and redemption.
Luckily, these mesmerizing performers could keep us enthralled through any of the cataclysmic events alluded to in the play.
It is, however, a quiet but exquisitely well-observed slice of life, set in an all-too-easily foreseeable future, when life itself has become, well, more thinly sliced.

But the actors’ fine efforts are not enough to fully breathe life into this willfully slow-paced, sluggish work, which treats minor domestic issues and the future of the planet with equal gravity.
That swirling unknown is bought startlingly to life at the end of the play, in one of the most visually stunning denouements on Broadway right now.

“Kirkwood's all too believable play about the aftermath of a nuclear accident, is much more than a cautionary dystopian tale...The intact transfer is a fortuitous one, resulting in a polished ensemble piece that captures a sense of the characters' history...
Having lived through an era of unprecedented peace and prosperity, Kirkwood’s characters are forced to confront the truth that all their efforts have bequeathed a blighted planet to their children.

Still, while it won't leave you smiling as you would after dinner with the reformed Scrooge or a replay of A Wonderful Life , The Children is indeed to be savored for its fine writing, direction, and acting.
The visually stylized, well-acted production is directed by James Macdonald.
Ultimately, this is a difficult piece of theater, and the ambiguous though beautiful ending (with evocative lighting by Peter Mumford) presents so many implications it makes the head spin.

Despite its title, The Children is the most adult show in New York City right now, a marvelously resonant, intelligent, and engaging play that continually defies expectations as the plot twists and turns while something threatening hangs just past the horizon.
What is truly marvelous is the gap between the comfortable dialogue between the twosome, and then the threesome, and the emotions snaking around and under them.
Director McDonald understands this balance of the quotidian with the apocalyptic, and keeps the action grounded in the rituals of daily life.
It’s a slow cooking machine here, but wildly satisfying in the end.
The imagery of the play, both in the physical setting and the playwright’s words, is stark and memorable.
Even with its occasional sluggish moments and some difficulty understanding the coastal English dialect, The Children has a fearful universality that lingers in the mind.
Kirkwood's drama is engrossing and absorbing.

“While the setup takes a while, the dénouement is worth waiting for, thanks greatly to the superb acting of the trio, Buether’s brilliant set, and truly illuminating lighting by Mumford...What did we just see, I asked upon exiting the theater.
Ms. Kirkwood's dialogue is sharp, funny, and somewhat spare, preferring suggestion over exposition.
For all its dramatic circumstances, The Children is not nearly as intense as its outline suggests.
As the play concludes, however, the story collapses in on itself.
Ms. Annis, Mr. Cook and Ms. Findlay are exquisite even when the material they have been given is not.

Kirkwood structures her compassionate, heart-wrenching treatise on social responsibility with such craft, you become wrapped up in the interrelations of this trio without even realizing they are symbols of modern society.
A play designed to disturb ends up producing an oddly lulling effect.
